frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d373:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the plenary session at Tehran on 30 November 1943 at four in the afternoon, the session at which the Overlord decision was announced to Stalin. Roosevelt opens by expressing his happiness at the decision reached that morning by the British and American staffs.

Brooke reports the agreement: Overlord will be launched during May 1944, with a supporting operation in southern France on as large a scale as landing craft allow. Stalin answers with the pledge he had already given the two leaders privately. Simultaneously with Overlord, the Red Army will launch large offensives at several points to pin German forces down and stop any transfer of troops westward. Roosevelt adds that the Overlord commander will be named within three or four days, and the Western staffs will return to Cairo the next day to work out the details.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d473:
Another message from President Roosevelt went to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on December 3, 1943, the day before the Second Cairo Conference opened. Roosevelt had finished at Tehran and was preparing to meet Churchill, and Turkey's President İnönü, at Cairo. The State Department kept the message in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Two presidential cables to Hull in a single day suggest how much unfinished business followed Roosevelt out of Tehran. Hull, in Washington, was the fixed point of American diplomacy while the President traveled. For the reader, this second message underlines the working partnership between the two men at a peak moment of the war.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d573:
Patrick J. Hurley, now ambassador to China, wrote to Secretary of State James F. Byrnes on August 11, 1945. Hurley had gone from the President's personal representative in Iran to the hardest embassy in Asia. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

August 11 fell in the war's last days: atomic bombs had fallen, the Soviet Union had entered the Pacific war, and Japan's surrender was days away. Hurley's China was sliding toward civil war even as the world war ended. For readers, his report connects the volume's long China thread, opened at Cairo in 1943, to the moment everything changed in Asia.
frus-1944-quebec-d73:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on August 28, 1944. His letter sits among the papers gathered for the Quebec Conference. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. Hull led the department that handled the alliance's daily diplomacy.

Letters from Hull to Roosevelt carried the department's view to the top. Two weeks later, the President would meet Churchill in Quebec City. The conference faced Germany's coming defeat and the Pacific war. For readers, the letter shows the State Department stating its position in writing. It did so before the leaders settled questions in person.
frus-1944-quebec-d173:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff opened their Quebec meetings at noon on September 12, 1944, with Sir Alan Brooke in the chair at Admiral Leahy's invitation. Early business was procedural: personnel shipping after Germany's defeat would be studied, and the conference program was approved. The chiefs then took up Eisenhower's appreciation, Scaf 78.

Brooke argued Eisenhower had understressed two points: opening Antwerp and Rotterdam, and a strong attack on the northern flank. He proposed an airborne operation to seize the Schelde islands guarding Antwerp. Marshall countered that German forces massed there, on coverless ground, made bombing more profitable than airborne troops. A draft reply approving Eisenhower's proposals, with the northern emphasis added, was presented for discussion.
frus-1944-quebec-d273:
Redeployment after the European war is the subject of C.C.S. 679, dated September 14, 1944. The United States Chiefs judged the whole problem, including repatriation, too large for the conference to settle. It needed combined study to assure the optimum use of personnel and cargo shipping, and to get forces against Japan to their theater at the earliest date.

They recommended the Combined Administrative Committee study and report on the problem, working with the transportation committee, the shipping authorities, and the staff planners. Questions needing earlier decision would go to the Combined Chiefs. The paper was approved the next day with Brooke's amendment adding the Combined Shipping Authorities to the list of collaborators.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d73:

The six items start with voting in the Security Council and who the first members would be. They go on to the seat of the new body and to trusteeship plans. The court statute and the ending of the League of Nations complete the list. Advice is attached on the first four. On the court, legal experts would draft the statute before the founding talks opened.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d173:

The item concerns Yugoslavia and the agreement lately drawn up between Marshal Tito and Premier Subasic, head of the exile government. Brigadier MacLean has told Ambassador Kirk the expected British course. Churchill will press King Peter to accept the agreement. Once it takes effect, Britain will send an ambassador to Belgrade. The short note marks how far Tito's partisans had come toward open allied backing.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d273:

At General Deane's request, Kennan had written to Molotov on 6 November about two-way arrangements for prisoners of war. Soviet armies had already overrun one camp known to have held Americans, and were closing on another near Budapest. Molotov's answer of 25 November is quoted in paraphrase. Moscow's first concern is help and homecoming for Soviet prisoners and for citizens deported by the Germans, now freed in the west. pare-deux-livres-chirurgie-1573:

ralston-russian-fairy-tales-1873:

kant-critique-practical-reason-abbott-18:
Immanuel Kant published the Critique of Practical Reason in 1788, his main work on moral philosophy. The English text here is T. K. Abbott's translation of 1873. Kant argues that moral law comes from reason itself, not from desire or reward. His categorical imperative bids us act only on rules we could will for all.

Persons, for Kant, must always be treated as ends, never merely as means. He links morality to freedom and to belief in God and immortality as hopes of reason. The book founded a major school of ethics centered on duty. Its claims still anchor debates in moral philosophy today.
kant-groundwork-abbott-1873:
Immanuel Kant published his Groundwork on morals in 1785, here under the title Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals. The English text is T. K. Abbott's translation of 1873. Kant seeks the supreme rule of morality in reason alone. Good will, he says, is the only thing good without limit.

He states the categorical imperative in several forms for clarity. Act only on maxims fit to be universal law, and treat humanity always as an end. Shorter and clearer than the Critiques, the Groundwork is widely taught. It is the classic statement of duty-based ethics. Students of philosophy still meet Kant first through these pages.
mill-autobiography-1873:
John Stuart Mill's Autobiography appeared in 1873, the year of his death. Mill tells the story of his remarkable education under his father, James Mill. Greek at three and logic in childhood formed a mind of rare power. The book then recounts his mental crisis in his twenties, when dry analysis failed him.

Poetry, above all Wordsworth, restored his feelings and saved his life. Mill describes his growth toward a softer, wider utilitarianism. He also honors Harriet Taylor, his wife and intellectual partner. The book is the classic intellectual autobiography in English. It shows both the cost and the glory of a life of thought.
bastiat-sophisms-stirling-1873:
Frederic Bastiat was a French writer who defended free trade with wit sharp enough to outlive his century. His Economic Sophisms, in Stirling's 1873 translation, collects short essays that mock the fallacies behind tariffs and protection. Each piece takes a popular error and walks it into absurdity.

The most famous piece is the candlemakers' petition, which asks the state to block the sun as unfair foreign competition. Another tells of a broken window, showing that repair spending is loss, not gain, once the unseen costs count. Free traders still quote Bastiat more than any other nineteenth-century writer.
hodge-systematic-theology-vol3-1873:
Volume three of Hodge's Systematic Theology, in this 1874 edition, crowns the Princeton system with eschatology, the doctrine of the last things. Hodge had covered God, man, and Christ's work in the earlier volumes. The aged professor writes here with a lifetime of teaching behind him.

He treats death, the soul's state after death, the return of Christ, resurrection, and the final judgment in ordered sequence. His method stays the same: gather the Bible's statements, sort them, and answer rival views with calm reason. Princeton's students received the volume as the completion of the great Calvinist system in America.
junctinus-speculum-astrologiae-1573:
Francesco Giuntini, known in Latin as Junctinus, was a Florentine Carmelite and astrologer to great houses. His Speculum Astrologiae, Mirror of Astrology, appeared in 1573. The massive commentary treats the casting and judgment of nativities, the birth charts on which the art staked its fame.

Junctinus gathers the rules of Ptolemy, the Arab masters, and the Latin tradition into one vast storehouse for the working astrologer. Kings and courtiers of his age kept such men close, and his book shows the learning their favor bought. Scholars of Renaissance astrology still quarry the Speculum for the tradition it preserves entire. The sheer size of the work is part of its claim on the reader.
maxwell-treatise-electricity-magnetism-v:

calderon-wonder-working-magician-maccart:

racine-athaliah-donkersley-1873:

riemann-hypotheses-geometry-clifford-187:

The President wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 1 August 1945. The cable went out on the summit's last full day. Truman's word to his China envoy joined the German endgame to the Asian war in one channel.

Hurley's mission needed the president's backing at that hour. China's government was weakening, Japan's defeat was near, and the shape of Asia hung on choices being made in both capitals. A note from the top set the envoy's line for the weeks ahead. This message shows the president closing his Potsdam work with an eye already on the next crisis.

The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

American proposals show what Washington chose to ask for in the open, in words the British and Soviets could accept or refuse. The Department of State sent a telegram to the American embassy in London on 12 September 1945. Department telegrams speak in the secretary's name to posts abroad. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A telegram to London in September 1945 belongs to the weeks when embassies were being told how the wartime secret work would change. London was the greatest of the wartime intelligence stations, so word sent there mattered. Readers can place this telegram at the head of the volume's file on the State Department's own intelligence service. It shows the department addressing its posts as it prepared to take in the analysts the president's order was about to give it.

The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Eddy) and the Assistant Secretary of State for Administration (Russell). The reader was Secretary of State Byrnes. It is document 173 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d273:

It stands as document 273 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.

By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. frus-1861-d73:
Frederick W. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 27 August 1861. The younger Seward served as Assistant Secretary of State under his father. The letter is document 73 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

When the Secretary was away or pressed, his son kept the London line open. The note shows the office working as a family shop in a crisis. It also spared Adams any gap in direction from Washington at a tense time. Frederick Seward later wrote the great memoir of his father's years in office. The son's hand kept the father's line unbroken through a crowded autumn.
frus-1861-d173:
Carl Schurz sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 August 1861. It is document 173 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By August, word of the Union defeat had reached Spain. Schurz had to face a court that now doubted Union strength. His report shows a young envoy learning to hold his ground with words when the news ran against him. A young envoy's growth, traced week by week, is one of this file's quiet pleasures. Growth of that kind, seen in real time, is a rare gift of a full record.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.

Congress received it as Document 73 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. On 17 October 1862 Charles Francis Adams sent a report from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 173 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams had held the London post since the spring of 1861.

The son and grandson of presidents, Adams kept a cool style in his official mail even when stakes were high. His reports mixed meeting notes with shrewd reads of British politics. A letter from this date belongs to the weeks when the British cabinet was quietly deciding against stepping into the war. That was the outcome Adams most wanted. The legation's clerks copied each dispatch into bound letter books before the mail sailed.
frus-1862-d273:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 5 May 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 273 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The same day, far away, Mexico's army won at Puebla.

The coincidence of dates is a reminder of how slowly news moved. Seward wrote in ignorance of the battle that would stall France in Mexico for a year. His letter belongs to the Washington-Paris routine of orders and arguments about the war. Read in sequence, such letters show policy being made on partial knowledge, then corrected by the next mail.
frus-1862-d373:

Prompt written answers were the State Department's way of keeping small matters small. In August 1862 that discipline mattered, because any dispute with a foreign representative could feed the larger debate over intervention. The Seward-Treilhard exchange, preserved in quick alternation, shows the method applied steadily through a tense month. The channel, like the British one, stayed open and civil through the whole of 1862. France and Britain consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d473:

Portugal was a small power with Atlantic islands and ports that mattered to wartime shipping, and its neutrality had to be exact. Harvey, a Pennsylvania editor turned diplomat, held the Lisbon post through the war. Seward's orders to such outposts dealt in the practical law of neutrality: what belligerent ships could take on, and how long they could stay. The dispatch begins the Portuguese correspondence, a minor file with real stakes for the blockade at sea.
frus-1862-d573:

December 1861 was the month of the Trent crisis. Seward's orders to distant posts had to assume their readers knew little of the latest turn. Brazil, an empire with Atlantic ports on the routes to the Pacific, had neutrality duties to define toward belligerent cruisers and prizes. Webb needed Washington's rules in writing. The instruction shows the Department reaching to the far end of its network. A letter there might take two months to arrive. It still had to govern conduct when it did.

By the spring of 1862 Burlingame had found his feet in the post. His mail reported on the treaty ports, the Qing court's straits, and the acts of the other foreign powers in China. Letters like this one were the State Department's eyes in East Asia. Kept in the printed volume, they still show how much of American policy rested on one envoy's word.
frus-1863p1-d73:

Adams wrote on the eve of a set piece in British public life: the opening of Parliament, set for the next day. His mail that week watched for what the Queen's speech and the houses would say of the war. Reports like this one told Washington how the land lay at the top of British power. It is a short step in the file from this letter to the famous one that follows it.
frus-1863p1-d173:

It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.

It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d573:

It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d673:
A dispatch dated 23 November 1863 went from Secretary William H. Seward to the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.

David R. Halpin and Pehr B. Harbury launched a three-part methods series in PLOS Biology in 2004. The first paper sets out DNA display, a way to route large mixed pools of DNA based on their sequences. Each DNA strand acts as a label that directs where its attached cargo goes.

Sorting molecules by sequence could let chemists run many reactions in one pot and still keep track of each product. That is the base idea behind DNA-encoded libraries, now a major tool in drug hunting. Part one lays the routing rules. Later parts build genetic handling and synthesis on top of them. The series is a blueprint, best read as one project in three steps.
plos-pbio-0020273:
Miria Ricchetti, Fredj Tekaia, and Bernard Dujon traced stray DNA in the human genome in PLOS Biology in 2004. Mitochondria, the cell's power plants, have their own small genome. Over time, chunks of that DNA have leaked into the main genome in the nucleus, and the authors show the process has not stopped.

Fresh insertions can still be told apart from ancient ones by their condition. Recent arrivals look nearly intact, while old ones have decayed. That ongoing traffic means our genome is still being edited by its own power plants. It also creates a trap for researchers. A test for mitochondrial DNA may pick up a nuclear copy by mistake. That is a real concern in disease and ancestry studies.

Esther Clarke, Ulrich H. Reichard, and Klaus Zuberbühler analyzed wild gibbon songs in PLOS ONE in 2006. Gibbons sing long, patterned duets at dawn. The authors broke those songs into units and asked whether the units combine by rules, like a simple syntax, and carry meaning for listeners.

plos-pone-0000173:

Resistance tests cost money up front but can steer patients to drugs that work. The authors model the balance of cost and benefit. Their analysis helps clinics and insurers decide when testing pays for itself, a practical question in HIV care where second-line drugs are far more expensive.
plos-pone-0000273:

Dam methylation was known to affect a handful of E. coli processes, from DNA copying to virulence in relatives. A genome-wide assessment separates its broad effects from its minor ones. The paper helps settle how central this chemical marking system is to a model bacterium's daily life.
plos-pone-0000373:
Carmen Capone and co-authors investigated cell therapy for stroke damage in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. They worked with cells grown from neurospheres, small balls of neural stem-like cells raised in the lab. The question was whether these cells can protect the brain after blood flow is blocked, the event known as ischemia.

Rather than replacing lost brain cells, the transplanted cells appear to protect by changing the damaged tissue around them, the ischemic microenvironment. That shift in thinking matters for therapy design: a cell treatment might help mainly by calming harmful conditions near the injury. The study adds to efforts to turn stem cell science into stroke treatments.
plos-pone-0000473:
Claudio Lunardi and colleagues linked antibodies against a common virus to blood vessel damage, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Human cytomegalovirus infects most adults quietly and stays for life. The team found that a subset of antibodies against it can activate endothelial cells. These cells line the blood vessels. The antibodies can also push them toward apoptosis, programmed death.

Injured vessel lining is an early step in atherosclerosis, the artery disease behind heart attacks and strokes. If antiviral antibodies cross-react with the vessel wall, a lifelong infection could quietly raise cardiovascular risk. The authors draw that relevance explicitly, proposing one route by which chronic infection may feed chronic disease.
plos-pone-0000573:
Melissa A. Fowler and colleagues mapped two channels' presence across the rodent brain's emotion circuits, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The channels are TRPC4 and TRPC5, which let ions into neurons and shape their firing. The team charted corticolimbic expression of both channels, in cortex and limbic areas that process emotion and memory.

An expression map tells researchers which circuits a channel could influence, from fear to reward. TRPC channels have been tied to anxiety-like behavior in animals, making their addresses relevant to drug hunting. Mapping studies like this precede any claim that blocking a channel would help the brain rather than harm it.
plos-pone-0000673:
Dominique Lévesque, Francis P. Brière and Jean-Pierre Perreault described a modern way of switching on nucleic acid enzymes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Enzymes evolved subtle activation modes to keep their targeting precise, as modern cell metabolism demands. One mode uses a target-dependent module, a docking domain that engages only when the right target appears. Such modules appear in small interfering RNAs and other systems.

Nucleic acid enzymes, made of DNA or RNA themselves, cut or join other nucleic acids. A docking-based switch keeps them off until their target is present. Understanding that design helps researchers build precise molecular tools, and it explains how cells avoid costly targeting mistakes.
plos-pone-0000773:
Ken Dawson-Scully, Gary A. B. Armstrong, Clement Kent and colleagues linked heat tolerance in nerves to one signaling enzyme, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genetic variation is known to contribute to individual differences in thermotolerance, the ability to withstand heat. The specific genes and pathways involved, and how the environment modulates them, remained poorly understood. The team connects natural variation in neural function and behavior under heat to a cGMP-dependent protein kinase.

An enzyme best known from learning and feeding studies thus also helps set heat limits. As climates warm, the genes behind thermal tolerance move from academic to urgent. Model animals reveal which pathways might help or fail first.
plos-pone-0000873:
Thomas Hansen, Line Olsen, Morten Lindow and colleagues searched for brain microRNAs tied to schizophrenia, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genes that code for proteins have long been the main target in schizophrenia genetics. MicroRNAs are short pieces of RNA that tune how genes are used, and they play a real part in brain growth and function.

That made microRNA genes fresh candidates for the search. The team focused on ones active in the brain and checked them for links to the illness. Work like this widens the hunt beyond protein genes alone. It also fits a view of schizophrenia as a disorder of how brain circuits are built and tuned.
plos-pone-0000973:
Kevin Langergraber, Heike Siedel, John Mitani and colleagues read the genetic signature of sex biased migration, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In many societies one sex leaves home to breed while the other stays. Patrilocal groups, where females move, include both chimpanzees and many human cultures.

The team compare DNA passed only through mothers with DNA passed only through fathers. Different migration by sex leaves opposite marks on those two records. Their study tests how clearly that signature shows in chimps and humans. A clear signature lets researchers read past social structure straight from present day genes.
plos-pone-0001073:
L. Niels Cornelisse, Ronald van Elburg, Rhiannon Meredith and colleagues filmed calcium surges in dendritic spines at high speed, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fast calcium changes in postsynaptic structures are crucial for synaptic plasticity, the tuning of connections that underlies learning. Most work had studied how calcium falls after a surge, not how it rises.

Using high speed two photon imaging, the team follow the rise in tiny dendritic spines. Rise speed sets how much calcium a spine's buffers must absorb, and how strong the signal becomes. Their work links the kinetics in a spine, a structure a micron wide, to the capacity of the whole synapse to change.
plos-pone-0001173:
Tuberculous meningitis, TB infection of the membranes around the brain, is a devastating condition that demands fast treatment. Rapid diagnosis remains elusive, since the standard smear test on spinal fluid misses most cases.

The MODS technique grows TB bacteria in liquid and watches for their distinctive growth under a microscope. The authors tested how well it identifies tuberculous meningitis. A faster, more sensitive test matters because every day of delay in starting chemotherapy raises the risk of death or lasting damage.
plos-pone-0001273:

plos-pone-0001373:

From that group, 411 women met the study rules, split into a young group and an older group. The authors compared which cancer pathways were off track in each group. Their work maps how tumor biology shifts with age. Those maps may help doctors match care to the age and type of each case.
plos-pone-0001473:
Matthew Lohse and Alexander Johnson wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two forms of a yeast that infects people. The yeast, Candida albicans, lives in the gut of most healthy people. Using both fly and mouse eater cells, they found the forms are eaten at unlike rates. That gap may help the yeast hide or spread in the host. The work shows a shape shift can change how the immune system sees a germ. It adds a twist to how this common yeast causes grave ills.
plos-pone-0001573:
Jennifer Hayden and Sarah Ades published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a stress factor that keeps the E. coli cell skin sound. A class of backup gene switches sense stress in the cell's outer skin. They show the factor is a must for keeping the cell skin intact in this germ too. Without it, the skin leaks and the cell fares poorly. Skin stress paths are drug targets, since our own cells lack them. Each firm fact here aids the hunt for new germ drugs.
plos-pone-0001673:
James P. Stewart, Anja Kipar, Helen Cox, and their co-authors studied airway responses to virus infection in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The focus is a family of messenger molecules called tachykinins. One of them, substance P, is a known driver of inflammation linked to nerve signals in the airways.

Earlier work on tachykinins in lung defense had centered on nerves. Stewart's team instead asked whether the airway lining itself, the epithelium, starts making tachykinins when a virus infects it. The full text gives the infection model, the molecule levels they measured, and where production rose. If the lining joins in, then airway inflammation has a local source that treatments for asthma and chest infections may need to address.
plos-pone-0001773:
Gerard A. J. Morris, Usman N. Ikumapayi, Martin Antonio, and their co-authors identified a new bacterial type from a sick baby in The Gambia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Molecular tests instead revealed a novel Campylobacter jejuni sequence type, a food-poisoning germ not previously recorded there. The full text gives the typing method and the sequence. One found case shows how much infection hides behind malaria diagnoses in West African clinics.
plos-pone-0001873:

plos-pone-0001973:

plos-pone-0002073:

plos-pone-0002173:

plos-pone-0002273:

plos-pone-0003273:
